title: StereoKG: Data-Driven Knowledge Graph Construction for Cultural Knowledge and Stereotypes
benchmark_measurement: The paper develops and evaluates 'StereoKG', a data-driven knowledge graph of cultural knowledge and stereotypes about social groups, including 5 religious groups and 5 nationalities. The benchmark measures the quality (coherence, completeness, domain-relevance) of these extracted stereotypes and evaluates whether integrating this knowledge into language models can improve performance on knowledge-crucial samples in downstream tasks, specifically hate speech detection and masked stereotype prediction.
findings: The study found that its data-driven pipeline could successfully extract a knowledge graph of stereotypes for 5 religious groups. Most stereotypes were evaluated as neutral or negative. Atheists had the highest proportion of negative stereotypes (51.0%), while Jews had the lowest (37.2%). Hindus had the smallest proportion of positive stereotypes (2.9%). Integrating this extracted knowledge into a RoBERTa model via intermediate training improved its cultural awareness, leading to better predictions on masked sentences requiring cultural knowledge (e.g., about Muslims and the Quran) and a slight improvement in classifying hate speech that relies on stereotypical knowledge.
references: Anurag Acharya, Kartik Talamadupula, and Mark A. Finlayson. 2020. An atlas of cultural commonsense for machine reasoning. CoRR, abs/2009.05664.
